_readme: content_md for Chapter 10. This is the closing chapter — more discussion-oriented than the rest, matching the source workbook's own structure (two of five sections are class discussions). Sassa: consider whether 10.2 and 10.4 should stay teacher-led discussions rather than fully self-paced, given they're designed as open reflection, not information delivery.

sections.10.0:
You've come a long way: from why money exists, through fiat's failures, to how Bitcoin actually works under the hood. This final chapter steps back and asks the bigger question the whole Diploma has been building toward — why does any of this actually matter for your life?

Activity: before reading on, spend a few minutes on "What Could a Bitcoin Future Look Like?" — imagine your own community five, ten years from now if Bitcoin adoption kept growing the way it has locally.
sections.10.1:
Chapter 4 introduced Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) briefly — digital versions of national currency, issued and directly controlled by a central bank, unlike the commercial bank deposits most digital money exists as today.

CBDCs are actively being piloted or researched in many countries. Supporters point to efficiency and financial inclusion for the unbanked. Critics point to the risk of total visibility into every transaction anyone makes, and the technical ability for a government to freeze funds or restrict what they can be spent on, directly and instantly. Both concerns are worth taking seriously rather than dismissing either side.
sections.10.2:
This section is a class discussion, not a reading — the question at its center: do you have the right to control your own money?

It's worth approaching honestly rather than performing the 'correct' Bitcoin answer. Some genuine tensions worth sitting with: financial privacy versus fighting crime and tax evasion; individual control versus collective safety nets; self-responsibility versus the real risk of losing everything to a lost key or a scam. Bitcoin doesn't resolve these tensions — it just shifts who's responsible for navigating them.
sections.10.3:
Drawing together everything from this Diploma, Bitcoin's core, concrete benefits: a fixed, verifiable supply that no institution can quietly inflate away; the ability to hold and send value without needing anyone's permission; genuine ownership without a third party who can freeze or seize it; and a growing real-world usability, visible in our own EkasiPay merchant network, not just as a distant idea.

None of these benefits are free of tradeoffs — Chapters 7 and 9 were honest about the real responsibility self-custody requires. The case for Bitcoin isn't that it's risk-free; it's that, weighed honestly, many people find those tradeoffs worth taking.
sections.10.4:
This closing discussion asks you to look back rather than forward: how did your own perspective on money change over this Diploma?

Most people start this course thinking about money as something fixed and given — just how things are. By this point, you've seen it's a designed system, with real history, real tradeoffs, and real alternatives. That shift in perspective — understanding that money could be different, and now having the tools to participate in that difference yourself — is the actual outcome this Diploma was built to create.

Congratulations on completing the Bitcoin Diploma. Talk to Sassa about your certificate and what comes next — including the Postgraduate track, if you want to go further.
